data.title: Crude Oil Advances As U.S.-Iran War Concerns Continue While Qatar Steps Up Mediation Efforts
data.description:
WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - Recovering from earlier losses in the session, crude oil prices have moved higher on Friday as signals of war risk continued after U.S. President Donald Trump refused to rule out renewing attacks on Iran. This overshadowed the positivity from reports hinting that Qatar is speeding up the efforts to clear way for U.S.-Iran peace process.

WTI Crude Oil for December delivery was last seen trading up by $0.46 (or 0.51%) at $90.98 per barrel

Investors are yet to receive clarity on how the U.S. administration plans to defuse the Middle East crisis and figure out a way to permanently end all hostilities with Iran.

Trump suffered a setback this week when the midterm election results showed that the Democratic party seized control of the House and Senate.

While Trump remarked that Iran was partly responsible for the jolt, U.S. Vice President JD Vance conceded that Iran war was the primary reason for the defeat.

The war with Iran, which began in late February and is in its ninth month now, has rattled energy markets around the world after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz.

Prior to the elections, reports indicated a possible renewal of attacks on Iran by the U.S. on a grand scale after the elections.

Defiant Iran responded by stating that Iran could combat any attack by any aggressor and would strike back, ignoring geographical boundaries.

However, the results indicated that public support shifted in favor of the Democrats as U.S. households could not bear the squeezing on their budgets due to oil-linked inflation as a consequence of the U.S.-Iran war that Trump started.

Despite conquering Congress, the Democrat-elects have to wait until January to assume office. This period offers more than 60 days for Trump to either carry out the attacks as planned or attempt to solve the crisis through negotiations or as a third option enforce the current economic blockade for an extended period without ordering withdrawal of troops.

Yesterday, Trump stated that the world will soon know his decision on the possibility of a deal with Iran. Declining to rule out military option, Trump maintained that he could destroy what is left of Iran.

Trump replaced White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller who was the Deputy Chief of Staff. Of note, in April, Miller remarked that if Iran refused a deal, the U.S. blockade could continue without an end. As a last resort, he also suggested the destruction of Iran's energy infrastructure.

Reuters reported, citing an Iranian official, that Iran had sent a nuclear proposal to the U.S. through Qatar, with a precondition that a discussion will not begin until Iran's conditions are met by the U.S.

While Iran wants the lifting of U.S. sanctions, release of frozen Iranian assets in foreign countries, and adequate compensation for war losses, the U.S. wants a halt to Iran's nuclear program.

Today, Qatar officially stated that the Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani had a discussion with Trump over phone about de-escalation.

Causes of concern continue to remain as the Strait of Hormuz shipping traffic is still under threat.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reported an explosion on an oil tanker on its port side, 16 nautical miles east of Khasab, Oman, in the Strait of Hormuz yesterday.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps announced that two oil tankers that tried to transit the Strait of Hormuz through unauthorized routes struck mines.

While one tanker was hit in the eastern part of the strait, the other was struck within the strait itself. Soon after hitting the mines, the vessels caught fire.

The IRGC re-asserted Iran's stance that the strait will remain closed until Iran's conditions are fully met.

Even while the uncertainty over the U.S. strategy to deal with Iran continued to add geopolitical risk premium and pushed oil prices higher, expectations on a possible diplomatic solution partly offset the fears.

Today's economic data in the U.S. revealed stronger-than-expected payroll numbers.

The U.S. dollar index was last seen trading at 102.28, up by 0.70 (or 0.69%) today.

data.title: Saudi National Accused of Bugging OpenAI's Office Pleads Not Guilty — WSJ
data.description:
By Maxwell Zeff

Abdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national accused of bugging a restricted OpenAI conference room, pleaded not guilty on Friday in a federal court in San Francisco.

Appearing before a U.S. magistrate judge for an arraignment hearing, Alfozan's lawyer, David W. Rizk, said his client would plead not guilty for the single count he has been charged with: intercepting oral communications. The maximum penalty for the charge is five years in prison and a fine of $250,000.

Alfozan is currently in federal custody, and is next scheduled to appear in court on Nov. 17.

Alfozan is accused of wrapping a thumb-sized circuit board and microphone in toilet paper and inserting the device behind a wall-mounted TV inside an executive conference room in OpenAI's office around Sept. 28, shortly before he was set to leave the country. The Saudi national had been an employee on OpenAI's product team since July 2025 until he was fired in October, the same day he was arrested and charged.

Prosecutors previously alleged Alfozan booked one-way plane tickets from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia via Istanbul for himself, his wife and their newborn son departing on Oct. 12. Alfozan's wife and son left without him shortly after his arrest, prosecutors said.

The wife and child's one-way plane tickets were initially paid for by the Saudi government, but that flight was canceled, prosecutors said. They were then rebooked on another one-way flight to Qatar, this time in business class, by a member of the Saudi military, the filing said.

Lawyers representing Alfozan said the military official was the brother-in-law of his wife, and that she left because of issues with her visa. Alfozan's lawyers previously said she planned to return to the U.S. to support her husband.

Write to Maxwell Zeff at maxwell.zeff@wsj.com

data.title: Canada Fiscal, Rate Policies Look to Be Working at Cross Purposes — Market Talk
data.description: Canadian fiscal and monetary policies could be working at cross purposes, the chief economist at BMO Capital Markets tells clients in his week-ending note. Douglas Porter says the annual Canadian government budget plan is "meatier" than expected and delivers a significant dollop of fiscal stimulus — so much so that BMO has upgraded its Canada GDP growth forecast in 2027 to 2% from 1.8%. Meanwhile, the Bank of Canada raised rates to deal with an elevated inflation forecast, and could hike again. "If that's not rowing in different directions, it's not at all obvious what would count as policy friction," Porter says. In addition, he adds, weak jobs data, a pullback in oil prices and the tech selloff could prompt BOC policymakers to reconsider whether another hike in December is required. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

data.title: Cross-Border Payments Firm Behneh Files for IPO
data.description:
By Katherine Hamilton

Behneh filed for an initial public offering.

The Singapore-based financial technology company plans to offer 5 million shares for $3 to $5 apiece.

It intends to trade on Nasdaq under the ticker BENE.

Behneh offers cross-border payments to retail and institutional clients, including collection on behalf and payment on behalf services.

Its core business facilitates international transfers and related payment processing services. In addition to remittances, Behneh has more recently expanded into providing advisory services.

Following a 2023 inspection, deficiencies were identified in Behneh's money laundering and terrorism defense controls. Issues included customer due diligence and wire-transfer compliance.

Behneh said it has since implemented remediation measures to strengthen its security and compliance measures.

In the six months ended April 30, 2026, one customer accounted for 85% of Behneh's revenue. Total revenue during that time increased 17% to $504,893, compared with the same period the year before.

data.title: The AI Crash Broke the Market. Here Are 3 Things That Decide What's Next. — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Martin Baccardax

Aristotle never said "nature abhors a vacuum," but his insistence that empty space must always be filled created the rule that Wall Street lives by.

The stock market, by the way, hates the rule but follows it anyway, filling up the blank days on economic calendars, the weekends, and the holidays with all sorts of theories, rumors, and wagers — many that send investors in the wrong direction.

And that puts the market's end-of-year run, which includes 34 full trading days and trio of early closures, back in focus — especially after Tuesday's midterm elections triggered this brutal AI sell-off.

There are effectively only three calendar items left that will either steady investors' nerves or deepen their jitters: Nvidia's third-quarter earnings update, the planned public listing of AI start-up Anthropic, and the Federal Reserve's December rate decision. And there's one subject that has been a point of discussion for months now: the Iran war.

First, though a look at this past week to understand what's at stake going forward: The Nasdaq Composite fell into correction territory and had its biggest loss in market value on record. Plus, the AI trade is still facing its biggest test since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022.

For Alex Guiliano, of Resonate Wealth Partners, there certainly is uncertainty and a good possibility of more losses.

"This is a stock market that is trying to figure out the right valuations for the AI trade and grappling with a swift sentiment shift after the midterm elections," said Guiliano, Resonate Wealth's chief investment officer.

Before and after 2018's midterms, "the stock market experienced significant volatility and declined nearly 20%, so there is a historical precedent for more downside risk ahead," he added.

The next leg lower isn't hard to visualize: the Nasdaq is now less than 1% higher than it was at the end of July. The S&P 500 is sitting on a loss of 1.1% for the second half of the year.

Democratic wins in key states, including in Georgia, Texas, and Ohio, will probably put restrictions on AI data centers. And the blue wave on Capitol Hill could mean a regulation crackdown for the market's most-important sector.

And Wall Street's appetite for the AI trade, in the form of Anthropic's $1.5 trillion IPO, will no doubt be tested, too.

The S&P 500 Information Technology sector, in fact, is trading at the lowest levels in six months, and the Communications Services sector is at its lowest levels of the year. Together, the two make up half of the S&P 500's $67.4 trillion in market value.

Fourth-quarter earnings for both should still be solid and contribute 45.4% of the $810 billion in collective S&P 500 profits expected over the three months.

But tech's share of the profits is starting to slow and so is the overall rate for broader earnings growth. LSEG data shows overall profits will rise by 35% this year but fall by more than half — to 16% — in the coming year.

That's pretty much in line with what Capital Economics' John Higgins is expecting.

"We think there is plenty of scope for the rout [in both sectors] to continue in 2027 even if there is a rebound before the end of this year," he said.

"But we would be surprised if there were ultimately as big peak-to-trough drawdowns [in the tech and communications services sectors] as there were after the dotcom bubble burst," said Higgins, whose title is chief economic adviser.

"That's because this time the rally is more 'fundamental' than 'speculative,' judging by the relative contributing of earnings and the price that investors were willing to pay for them."

So back to the future: Nvidia's earnings are Nov. 17, Anthropic's IPO should come later this month, maybe before Thanksgiving, and the Fed's next policy meeting is Dec. 9. And the Iran war is in a holding pattern, for now.

Investors have to think about all of these things.

They even put the chances of an escalation in war behind them, either, even with last week's 14% slide in Brent crude prices, the largest in more than six years.

Nor can they discount the impact oil will have on inflation readings and, by extension, the Fed's final rate decision of the year.

Which, for ING economist James Smith, may now be cast in a very different light because of how the central bank's chairman, Kevin Warsh, is thinking.

"The rout in AI stocks matters because Warsh has rationalized a decent chunk of the Fed's rate hikes through loose financial conditions, widely seen as a euphemism for soaring equity prices," he said. "That's clearly changing. And a much deeper correction could raise serious doubts about another December hike."

Friday's strong jobs report, however, has kept the rate-hike heat at a simmer. The odds of a quarter-point increase, which would take the target to 4%-nd 4.25%, now stand at 80%, according to the CME FedWatch.

But, as Hirtle & Co.'s Brad Conger points out, the jobs report and the Fed projections are running a distant second to the market's AI trade — and there are few, if any, answers as to where that's headed.

"Under normal circumstances, an unexpectedly strong jobs report would crush Treasuries and lift rate hike expectations, but given the rout in the AI capex sectors over the past couple of weeks, all data points will be considered extremely 'backward looking'.

"All eyes are, rightly, are on the semiconductor stocks and the Anthropic IPO," said Cooper, who is Hirtle's chief investment officer.

In other words, chips and one very big public debut are what will fill the empty space.

November is historically the market's strongest month, with an average gain of 1.9% and upside moves 70% of the time since 1950, according to the Stock Trader's Almanac.

Maybe that will calm those late-autumn jitters, maybe not. But investors could use history repeating itself right about now.

Write to Martin Baccardax at martin.baccardax@barrons.com

data.title: Wall Street stocks in relief rally after heavy AI-related selloff
data.description:
Key points:
  • Benchmark S&P 500 and Nasdaq rise; Dow edges lower
  • Japan, Korea, Taiwan plunged in Asia, European stocks fall
  • Bonds take breather as US payrolls top forecasts
  • Oil set for biggest weekly drop since COVID plunge

By Chibuike Oguh and Marc Jones

Wall Street equities mostly rallied on Friday, reversing course after trillions of dollars of world stock market value was wiped out over fears that Democratic election victories this week would bring tighter US regulations for the AI industry.

Benchmark S&P 500 and the Nasdaq were trading higher with technology, communication services and consumer discretionary stocks driving gains. The Dow edged lower on the day. All three indexes were on track for weekly losses following a brutal selloff in the prior session.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.08%, the S&P 500 CBOE:SPX rose 0.71%, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.4%.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index was up 4.2% after slumping in its biggest one-day drop since April 2025. Nvidia rose 3%, after suffering its worst day since January 2025, when the emergence of low-cost Chinese AI model DeepSeek hammered markets.

Other heavyweight chipmakers, including AMD , Intel , and Micron Technology , were up between 5.5% and 10%, while Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX were also up 2% and 8% respectively after losses earlier this week.

"Most of the disruption of the AI buildout will not probably occur but it's just the uncertainty of the change in government from Republican-led to Democratic-led, not only at the federal level but the state, local levels," said Gerry Sparrow, president and portfolio manager at Sparrow Capital Management.

"That's causing some disruption in the expectations of investors... The volatility around elections or any political event, whether it be war or terrorist attack, is always going to disrupt the market."

Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa said on Thursday that the state — which already has a large share of US data centres — will introduce new laws to protect local communities from their further mass buildup.

The jitters are hitting an AI trade already under pressure from fears that the massive cost of the data centres and other infrastructure will limit future returns, spurring margin calls and spooking retail investors and hedge funds alike.

RIPPLE EFFECT

The bounces were in stark contrast with market action in the rest of the world. Europe's STOXX 600 lost 1%. In Asia, Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's KOSPI both slumped about 6%. For the Nikkei — just like Wall Street the previous day — it was the biggest one-day drop since US President Donald Trump's "Liberation Day" trade tariff panic of April 2025.

The MSCI All-World index EURONEXT:IACWI fell 0.52% while MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan (.MISX00000PUS) lost 3%.

PAYROLLS BEAT FORECASTS

US nonfarm payrolls, usually one of the most-focused on pieces of data, but largely overshadowed by the tech drama, showed a stronger-than-expected 165,000 pickup in jobs.

An anticipated slowdown in annual wage growth to below 3% for the first time in nearly 5-1/2 years did not materialise either as it came in at 3.1%.

The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note ticked up to 4.85%, having dropped to its lowest level since September 9 overnight.

In currencies, the dollar rose against major currencies including the euro, yen and Swiss franc. It was up 0.52% against the yen and rose 0.47% against the Swiss franc . The euro was down 0.68% against the dollar at $1.1142.

Brent crude prices tiptoed back up towards $100 a barrel, but are still set for their biggest weekly drop since 2020 on hopes the midterms' results might prompt Trump to de-escalate the Iran war.

Spot gold fell 0.48% to $4,067.75.

data.title: The Andersons to Acquire Harvestone Low Carbon Partners for $915 Million
data.description:
The Andersons agreed to acquire Harvestone Low Carbon Partners for $915 million, adding three ethanol production facilities with combined annual capacity of about 215 million gallons. The company also secured a long-term debt financing commitment from U.S. Bank and Farm Credit Mid-America, and expects to use its existing revolving credit facility as part of the funding. The acquisition is expected to close in late 2026 or early 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and other closing conditions.

Agreement 1: The Andersons to Acquire Harvestone Low Carbon Partners for $915 Million

  • Counterparty: Harvestone Low Carbon Partners and ECP V-B, ECP V-C and ECP V-D

  • Reason: Expand low-carbon ethanol production capacity

data.title: CBOT corn creeps higher before USDA crop data next week
data.description:
Chicago Board of Trade corn futures finished slightly higher on short covering and technical buying on Friday in a rebound from four-month lows reached this week, analysts said.

  • Traders were waiting for the US Department of Agriculture to update crop estimates in a monthly report due on Tuesday.

  • The USDA will use an artificial intelligence tool to check next week's crop production report after errors in corn data from September, agency officials said.

  • The USDA is expected to peg the nation's corn harvest at 15.962 billion bushels, down from its October estimate of 16.034 billion, according to a Reuters poll of analysts.

  • The harvest would be the second largest in history, after last year's record crop.

  • Drier weather will be favorable for farmers' remaining corn and soybean harvests next week, after rains delayed harvesting in some areas this week, forecasters said.

  • CBOT December corn (CZ26) ended up 1-1/2 cents at $4.41-1/2 per bushel after falling earlier to $4.38-1/2, which matched a four-month low set on Wednesday.

  • For the week, the contract dropped about 1.4%.
